passages.t: Haman promoted, and Mordecai will not bow
passages.happening:
‘After these events, King Xerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, elevating him to a position above all the princes who were with him’ (verse 1). The king commands that everyone at his gate bow to Haman. ‘But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage’ (verse 2).

The royal servants ask him why he disobeys the king's command. Day after day they warn him, and he will not do it, so they report him to Haman, ‘since he had told them he was a Jew’ (verse 4).

‘When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, he was filled with rage’ (verse 5). And when he learns who Mordecai's people are, ‘he scorned the notion of laying hands on Mordecai alone. Instead, he sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 ended with Mordecai saving the king's life and receiving nothing. Chapter 3 opens, with bitter irony, with someone else promoted: Haman, of whom nothing has been said before.

Haman is an Agagite. Most readers connect the name with Agag, king of the Amalekites, whom Saul spared against God's command. The Amalekites had attacked Israel on the road out of Egypt. Mordecai, a Benjaminite descended from a man named Kish, the name of Saul's father, now faces a descendant of Agag, or so many readers hear it. The book does not spell it out.

Bowing to a superior was ordinary courtesy in the ancient Near East, and Israelites bowed to kings and to one another without any thought of idolatry. So Mordecai's refusal needs an explanation, and the text gives only a hint: he tells the servants that he is a Jew.

Then comes the leap. In a single verse, a personal slight becomes a plan to destroy an entire people. The chapter traces how wounded pride, given power, can turn into hatred written into law.
passages.later: The old enmity begins in Exodus: ‘The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation’ (Exodus 17:16). And Saul ‘captured Agag king of Amalek alive’ (1 Samuel 15:8). No people living today is Amalek, and that old enmity gives no one a reason for contempt toward any people.
passages.hard:
Why did Mordecai refuse to bow to Haman, when Israelites bowed to kings and officials elsewhere in the Bible?

The Hebrew text does not say directly. Several explanations have been offered. One is that Haman claimed honor that belonged only to God, perhaps as part of a Persian court custom that the Greeks thought treated the king as almost divine. The Greek additions to Esther include a prayer of Mordecai saying that he refused so as not to set a human being's glory above God's. A second explanation is history: as a Benjaminite whose family recalled Saul's, Mordecai would not bow to a descendant of Agag. A third sees stubborn pride in Mordecai, noting that his refusal put his whole people in danger.

The text's only clue is that Mordecai explained his refusal by saying that he was a Jew, which points to a reason rooted in his faith and identity rather than personal dislike. Many interpreters combine the first two explanations. What the book makes plain is that Haman's response, to plan the destruction of a whole people for one man's refusal, is monstrous whatever Mordecai's reasons were.
passages.asks: One man's refusal to bow became, in Haman's heart, a reason to hate a whole people. Ask whether a grudge against one person has ever turned in you into contempt for a whole group. And ask what you would refuse to bow to, whatever it cost.

passages.t: A lot cast, and a decree sealed
passages.happening:
‘In the twelfth year of King Xerxes, in the first month, the month of Nisan, the Pur (that is, the lot) was cast before Haman to determine a day and month. And the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar’ (verse 7).

Haman goes to the king. “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws. So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them” (verse 8). He asks for a decree to destroy them, and offers ten thousand talents of silver to the royal treasury. The king hands him his signet ring. “Keep your money,” said the king to Haman. “These people are given to you to do with them as you please” (verse 11).

Letters go out in the king's name, sealed with his ring, to every province, in every script and language, ordering that all the Jews be destroyed and their goods plundered on a single day, the thirteenth of Adar (verses 12-13). ‘Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The lot is cast in the first month of Xerxes' twelfth year, about 474 BC, five years after Esther became queen. It falls on the twelfth month, nearly a year away. Ancient readers would have seen that delay as a disastrous choice for Haman, because it left time for a response.

Pur is related to an Akkadian word for lot. Casting lots to find a favorable day was a common practice in the ancient world, where people believed the gods showed good times through such means. The feast of Purim will take its name from it.

Haman's speech is a masterpiece of manipulation. He never names the Jews. He mixes a half-truth, that their laws are different, with a lie, that they do not keep the king's laws, and he appeals to the king's interests and his treasury. Ten thousand talents of silver was a staggering sum. The king does not even ask which people he is condemning.

The signet ring carried the king's seal. Handing it to Haman gave him power to issue decrees in the king's name. The decree is written on the thirteenth of Nisan, the day before Passover, the feast when Israel remembered how God rescued them from a foreign king.

The last verse sets two scenes side by side: the king and Haman drinking, and the city in confusion. The book does not linger over what the decree commands, and neither do these notes.
passages.later: The wisdom of Proverbs says who governs the lot: ‘The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD’ (Proverbs 16:33).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take a decree to destroy a whole people?

The chapter shows hatred of the Jewish people arising suddenly and being written into law, and it holds that hatred up to be seen for what it is. Haman's words, a certain people whose laws are different, are the words of a man looking for a reason to destroy. The book exposes them; it does not share them.

The threat to the Jews in Esther was a threat to the people through whom God had made his promises, and readers have long set it beside other moments when that people was in danger. But the point for any reader today is plain. Nothing in this chapter, or anywhere in Esther, is ever a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, or to harm anyone.
passages.asks: The king did not ask which people he was condemning, and then he sat down to drink. Ask where you have agreed to something without asking who would be hurt by it. And ask how you answer when someone says of a group of people, they are different, and they are a danger.
